Use the **right-hand grip rule**: the field circles the wire, and above it points towards
the north.
**Step 1 — grip the wire.** Point the right thumb along the current - **towards the
west** ✓ The fingers then curl in the direction of the magnetic field.
**Step 2 — read the field above the wire.** With the thumb west, the fingers pass
**northwards above** the wire and southwards below it ✓
So the field at a point **above** the conductor points **towards the north** ✓
**Step 3 — confirm with the vector form.** Take east as +x, north as +y and up as +z.
The current direction is Î = (−1, 0, 0) and the point above is along r̂ = (0, 0, 1):
B̄ ∝ Î x r̂ = (−1, 0, 0) x (0, 0, 1) = **(0, 1, 0)** ✓
the +y direction - **north** ✓
**The field below the wire.** By the same rule it points **south** ✓ The field encircles
the wire, so it reverses between points above and below.
**The magnitude.** For a long straight wire,
B = μ₀I/(2πr) ✓
falling off as 1/r, so the direction is the same at all heights above the wire but the
strength diminishes.
**A practical check - Oersted's experiment.** A compass needle held **above** a wire
carrying current deflects ✓ It was this chance observation in 1820 that first linked
electricity and magnetism, and the deflection direction is exactly what the grip rule
predicts.
**A caution about the Earth's field.** A real compass responds to the **resultant** of
the wire's field and the Earth's horizontal field ✓ The question asks only for the
field **due to the conductor**, which is purely north here.
**The alternative mnemonic.** Point the right thumb along the current and the curled
fingers give B; or use the **screw rule** - turn a right-handed screw so it advances
along the current, and its rotation gives the field ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **Towards south** ✗ is the field **below** the wire.
**East** and **west** ✗ lie along the wire itself, and the field is always
**perpendicular** to the current ✓
∴ towards north.

Charge leaks away fastest from **sharp points**, so the shape with no points at all holds
its charge longest.
**Step 1 — recall how charge distributes itself.** On a charged conductor the surface
charge density is **greatest where the curvature is greatest** ✓ Sharp points concentrate
charge; flat or gently curved surfaces spread it out.
**Step 2 — see what high charge density does.** The field just outside is
E = σ/ε₀ ✓
so a sharp point produces an intense local field. If it exceeds about **3 x 10⁶ V m⁻¹**,
the air **ionises** and charge streams away - **corona discharge**, or the "action of
points".
**Step 3 — compare the four shapes.**
**sphere** - uniform curvature, **no** point of concentration; charge density is the same
everywhere ✓ the slowest leakage
**cylinder** - has edges at its ends, where charge concentrates
**pear** - has a pronounced narrow end, a region of high curvature
**lightning conductor** - a deliberately **sharp spike**, designed to leak charge as fast
as possible ✓ the very worst choice here
**Step 4 — conclude.** The **sphere** retains charge longest ✓
**Why the sphere is uniform.** Symmetry: no part of its surface differs from any other ✓
so the charge has no reason to prefer one region, and σ is constant everywhere.
**Why lightning conductors are pointed.** Precisely to exploit the opposite effect ✓
The sharp tip ionises the air around it and quietly discharges the cloud's induced
charge, or else offers the strike a preferred, safely earthed path.
**Where the sphere is used in practice.** The dome of a **Van de Graaff generator** is a
large smooth sphere ✓ Its size and smoothness keep σ - and hence the surface field -
low, allowing enormous potentials to be held without breakdown. Any nick or scratch on
it causes leakage at once.
**The quantitative statement.** For two connected spheres of radii r₁ and r₂,
σ₁/σ₂ = r₂/r₁ ✓ so the **smaller** sphere - the sharper surface - carries the higher
density. A point is the limit of a very small radius.
∴ a sphere.

The potential of a charged conductor depends on **how much charge** it carries **and on
its shape and size**.
**Step 1 — write the relation.**
V = Q/C ✓
so the potential depends on both the charge Q and the capacitance C.
**Step 2 — see what C depends on.** Capacitance is purely **geometrical** ✓ For an
isolated sphere,
C = 4πε₀R
so a bigger sphere has a larger capacitance and reaches a **lower** potential for the
same charge.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Both the **amount of charge** and the **geometry and size** of
the conductor matter, so the answer is **both** ✓
**A worked comparison.** Give 1 µC to two spheres:
radius 0·1 m: C = 4πε₀(0·1) = 1·11 x 10⁻¹¹ F, so V = **90 kV**
radius 1·0 m: C = 1·11 x 10⁻¹⁰ F, so V = **9 kV** ✓
The same charge, a tenfold difference in potential - the geometry is decisive.
**Why shape matters as well as size.** A long thin wire and a compact sphere of the same
surface area have quite different capacitances ✓ Capacitance depends on the whole
geometry, not on any single dimension.
**The practical consequence.** A Van de Graaff generator is built with the **largest
possible** dome ✓ A large C means more charge can be accumulated before the potential
reaches the breakdown field of the surrounding air.
**The related effect in a connected pair.** Join a large and a small sphere by a wire and
they come to the **same potential**, but the larger one takes **most of the charge** ✓
since Q = CV and C is larger. This is why charge concentrates on the broad parts of an
irregular conductor.
**Why neither option alone is enough.** Doubling the charge doubles the potential; so
does halving the size ✓ Each factor changes V independently, so neither can be dropped.
**Reading the distractors.** "**Only the amount of charge**" ✗ and "**only (1)**" ✗ both
ignore the capacitance. "**Geometry and size**" alone ✗ ignores the charge - an uncharged
conductor of any shape sits at zero potential ✓
∴ both (1) and (2).

The inductor and capacitor voltages are **in antiphase**, so they subtract before the
resistor's voltage is added in quadrature.
**Step 1 — combine V_L and V_C.** They differ in phase by 180°:
V_L − V_C = 60 − 30
= **30 V** ✓
**Step 2 — add V_R in quadrature.** The net reactive voltage is perpendicular to V_R in
the phasor diagram:
V = √(V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²)
= √(40² + 30²)
= √(1600 + 900)
= √2500
= **50 V** ✓
**Why the three voltages do not simply add.** Each is a **phasor**, not a scalar ✓
V_R is in phase with the current
V_L **leads** the current by 90°
V_C **lags** it by 90°
so V_L and V_C point in exactly opposite directions and cancel to the extent of 30 V.
**Why 130 V is wrong.** It is the arithmetic sum 60 + 30 + 40 ✗ which would require all
three to be in phase - they are not, and the question is built to catch exactly that ✓
**The 3-4-5 triangle.** V_R = 40 and the net reactive 30 are the legs of a right triangle
scaled by 10, giving a hypotenuse of **50** ✓
**The phase angle.**
tan φ = (V_L − V_C)/V_R = 30/40 = 0·75
**φ = 36·9°**, with the current **lagging** the supply voltage since V_L > V_C ✓ the
circuit is net inductive.
**A striking feature of LCR circuits.** The 60 V across the inductor **exceeds** the 50 V
supply ✓ This is perfectly normal - the inductor and capacitor voltages can each be
many times the source voltage near resonance, which is why components in resonant
circuits must be rated carefully.
**What would happen at resonance.** V_L would equal V_C, they would cancel entirely, and
the supply voltage would be just V_R ✓ with the current at its maximum.
**Reading the distractors.** **70 V** ✗ is 40 + 30, adding the resistive and net
reactive voltages as scalars. **10 V** ✗ is 40 − 30 ✓
∴ 50 V.

Connecting the capacitors in **parallel** brings them to a common potential, and energy
is **lost** in the process.
**Step 1 — find the common potential.** Charge is conserved, and the two are now in
parallel:
V = (C₁V₁ + C₂V₂)/(C₁ + C₂)
= [5(2000) + 5(1000)]/(5 + 5)
= 15000/10
= **1500 V** ✓
**Step 2 — compute the energy before.**
U_i = ½C₁V₁² + ½C₂V₂²
= ½(5 x 10⁻⁶)(2000²) + ½(5 x 10⁻⁶)(1000²)
= 10 + 2·5
= **12·5 J**
**Step 3 — compute the energy after.**
U_f = ½(C₁ + C₂)V²
= ½(10 x 10⁻⁶)(1500²)
= **11·25 J**
**Step 4 — find the loss.**
ΔU = 12·5 − 11·25
= **1·25 J** ✓
**The direct formula.** For two capacitors joined with like plates together,
ΔU = ½ [C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂)](V₁ − V₂)² ✓
= ½(2·5 x 10⁻⁶)(1000)²
= **1·25 J** ✓ in one line, and it shows that the loss depends on the **square of the
potential difference** between them.
**Where the lost energy goes.** Into **heat in the connecting wires** and, if the
transfer is rapid, into **electromagnetic radiation** ✓ The loss is unavoidable: even
with zero resistance, the charge redistribution radiates. It is one of the standard
puzzles of elementary electrostatics.
**Why there is always a loss when V₁ ≠ V₂.** The formula contains (V₁ − V₂)², which is
positive unless the potentials are equal ✓ Only capacitors already at the same potential
can be joined without loss.
**Why charge is conserved but energy is not.** Charge cannot be created or destroyed, so
the total is fixed at 15 mC ✓ Energy, by contrast, can be **converted** - and here part
of it leaves the capacitors altogether.
**Reading the distractors.** **5 J** ✗ and **160 J** ✗ exceed the total energy initially
stored, 12·5 J - impossible. **0 J** ✗ would require the two to be already at the same
potential ✓
∴ 1.25 J.

Conductor C is pulled both ways; find each force and subtract.
**Step 1 — write the force per unit length between parallel currents.**
F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)
= **2 x 10⁻⁷ I₁I₂/d** ✓
and since all three currents flow in the **same** direction, every pair **attracts**.
**Step 2 — find the attraction towards A.** A carries 2 A, C carries 3 A, and they are
5 cm apart:
F_A = 2 x 10⁻⁷ x (2)(3)/0·05
= 2 x 10⁻⁷ x 120
= **2·4 x 10⁻⁵ N** per metre, directed **towards A** ✓
**Step 3 — find the attraction towards B.** B carries 4 A and is 8 cm from C:
F_B = 2 x 10⁻⁷ x (3)(4)/0·08
= 2 x 10⁻⁷ x 150
= **3·0 x 10⁻⁵ N** per metre, directed **towards B** ✓
**Step 4 — take the resultant.** The two pull in **opposite** directions:
F = 3·0 x 10⁻⁵ − 2·4 x 10⁻⁵
= **0·6 x 10⁻⁵ N**, towards **B** ✓
**Step 5 — note the length.** C is **1 m** long, so the force per metre is the whole
force ✓
**Why B wins despite being further away.** It carries twice A's current, and the force
goes as the **product** of the currents but only as **1/d** ✓ Here 4/8 = 0·5 beats
2/5 = 0·4, so B's pull is the stronger.
**Where the balance point would be.** Setting the two equal, with x the distance from A
and 13 − x from B:
2/x = 4/(13 − x) → 26 − 2x = 4x → **x = 4·33 cm** ✓
If C sat 4·33 cm from A it would feel **no** net force - slightly closer to A than its
actual 5 cm, which is why the pull towards B wins.
**Why parallel currents attract.** Each wire sits in the other's magnetic field, and
F̄ = I L̄ x B̄ works out **inward** for currents in the same sense ✓ Antiparallel currents
repel - which is why the definition of the ampere is framed in terms of this force.
**Reading the distractors.** **5·4 x 10⁻⁵ N** ✗ is the **sum** 2·4 + 3·0, which would be
right only if the forces acted the same way - that is, if one current were reversed.
Its direction, towards A or B, is immaterial once the subtraction is seen ✓
∴ towards B equal to 0.6 × 10⁻⁵ N.
